children: RBI rate hike expectations are rising as inflation pressures build, with Axis Capital saying an October move could become necessary if the Fed hikes rates

The case for an October rate hike by the Reserve Bank of India is gaining strength as headline inflation rises and underlying price pressures edge higher, according to an Axis Capital research report. However, the report said the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) would ideally remain on hold in October, with a December hike forming its base case.

India’s retail headline inflation rose 37 basis points to 4.8 per cent year-on-year in August from 4.5 per cent in July, in line with expectations. The increase was led by higher food prices, while core inflation also rose 27 basis points. Food inflation increased to 5.7 per cent in August from 5.2 per cent in July.

Axis Capital said vegetables, pulses and fruits remain vulnerable to monsoon-related risks, with rainfall trends over the coming weeks likely to remain important for the inflation outlook. Sugar prices were also 11 per cent higher year-on-year in August.

The report said core services inflation has been steadily climbing and stood at 3.9 per cent. Its preferred measure of demand-side inflation indicated underlying price pressures at around 3.5 per cent and rising rapidly.

Axis Capital noted that headline inflation has risen 1.4 percentage points between March and August, with food, transport and restaurant services accounting for most of the increase. Food contributed 72 basis points, transport 40 basis points and restaurant services 18 basis points.
Fed Decision Key To RBI Move

Axis Capital expects the RBI to raise rates at its December MPC meeting but said an earlier move could become necessary if the US Federal Reserve raises rates. Markets were assigning a 92 per cent probability to a Fed hike, although that was not Axis Capital’s base case. A US rate increase could put pressure on the RBI to respond, particularly if higher energy prices create persistent inflationary pressures.

The report also flagged geopolitical developments around the Strait as a key risk. It said tightening monetary policy during an adverse energy shock can hurt growth, but may become necessary if a temporary price shock develops into persistent, broad-based inflation.
